Used
uzd
v. (employed; put to service; and in the older idiom, accustomed or habituated)
From use, Latin uti, to employ. The Authorized Version carries two senses that modern English has separated: employed, and was accustomed to — as in so used the young men to do.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version uses this plain word twenty-one times, and the range is worth noticing because it is almost entirely moral. It is the word for what men habitually do: “the disciples of John and of the Pharisees used to fast” (Mar 2:18) — the older English sense of were accustomed. It is the word for the forbidden arts: Manasseh and the northern kingdom alike “used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger” (2Ki 17:17). It is the word for institutional cruelty: “The people of the land have used oppression, and exercised robbery, and have vexed the poor and needy: yea, they have oppressed the stranger wrongfully” (Eze 22:29) — oppression as a practice, something a nation uses the way a craftsman uses a tool. And it is the word for how God has spoken to His people: “I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets” (Hos 12:10). That last is a striking admission of divine method — God has deliberately used likenesses, figures, and comparisons, through men, because that is how He chose to be understood.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines used as employed; accustomed; and notes the participial sense of being habituated or inured to a thing.

expand to see more

U'SED, pp. Employed; accustomed.

U'SE, v.t. s as z. [L. utor, usus.]

1. To employ; to handle, hold or move for some purpose.

2. To make use of; to convert to one's service.

3. To accustom; to habituate; to render familiar by practice. So used the young men to do. Judges 14. In this sense it is now chiefly used in the past tense, as, he used to walk.

Key Scripture

Hosea 12:10 — "I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets."

2 Kings 17:17 — "And they caused their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire, and used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger."

Ezekiel 22:29 — "The people of the land have used oppression, and exercised robbery, and have vexed the poor and needy: yea, they have oppressed the stranger wrongfully."

Mark 2:18 — "And the disciples of John and of the Pharisees used to fast: and they come and say unto him, Why do the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, but thy disciples fast not?"

Modern Corruption

Hosea 12:10 is pressed to make the prophets mythmakers, as though God's use of figures made the history figurative.

expand to see more

I have… used similitudes is a favourite text of those who wish the historical narratives of Scripture to be understood as parable — a literary mode rather than a record. The verse says something narrower and more useful: that God employed likenesses through the ministry of the prophets. Hosea himself is a case in point, since his marriage was both a real marriage and a figure of Israel's adultery, and the figure has its force precisely because the history is real. Divine accommodation in language is not divine fiction in fact. The dictionary holds the ordinary Reformed rule: the literal sense is the sense the author intended, which includes figures where figures are used and history where history is written.

2 Kings 17:17 shows the word doing darker work, and it is worth pausing on. Divination and enchantment are described as things men used — instruments, techniques, methods for getting leverage over the future. That is the abiding appeal of the occult in every age, including this one, where it returns as astrology, manifestation, and the various therapeutic spiritualities. The biblical objection is not that such things never produce an effect but that they are an attempt to obtain from somewhere else what God has reserved to Himself, and the verse names the outcome plainly: sold themselves to do evil.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew damah (H1819), to liken, compare; nachash (H5172), to practise divination; Greek esan nesteuontes, were fasting; Latin uti, to employ.

expand to see more

Hebrew adammeh (H1819) — I will liken, use similitudes; Hosea 12:10, God's own account of His method.

Hebrew nechashim (H5172) — divinations, enchantments; 2 Kings 17:17, techniques for compelling the future.

Hebrew osheq (H6233) — oppression, extortion; Ezekiel 22:29, a practice the people of the land used.

Hebrew ger (H1616) — the stranger, sojourner; the party oppressed wrongfully in the same verse.

Latin uti, usus — to employ, employed; Webster's root behind both English senses.

Usage

"“I… used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets” — accommodation in language, not fiction in fact."

"“Used divination and enchantments” — the occult as technique, in any century."

"“Used to fast” — the older English for were accustomed."
